tagline: The Amazon's river-bus metropolis — a 1.3-million-person capital where the boat already does the metro's job, freshly rebuilt for COP30 with three new waterfront terminals and a bay full of island lines waiting to fly.
summary: Belém sits on the Baía do Guajará at the mouth of the Amazon, and here the water is not a leisure amenity — it is the road. Students, workers, restaurant-goers and entire island communities move daily by lancha between the capital, the forested restaurant island of Combu, car-free Cotijuba, the beach island of Mosqueiro, the industrial hub of Barcarena and the buffalo island of Marajó. Hosting COP30 in November 2025 triggered a once-in-a-generation waterfront rebuild — a R$53M state terminal, two brand-new terminals at Icoaraci and Tamandaré, and the R$568M Porto Futuro II restoration — so the piers are new while the fleet is still slow diesel. A silent, zero-wake foiling layer would modernise a water-transit habit this city has had for a century, right where the world just watched a climate conference.

demand_signals.label: State waterway ridership
demand_signals.value: 553,823 passengers in 2024 on Pará's intermunicipal waterway system — 52 regular lines, 80 operators, 268 vessels, 43 terminals
demand_signals.note: Top lines all touch Belém: Belém–Barcarena, Icoaraci–Camará (Marajó), Belém–Breves, Belém–Soure, Ponta de Pedras–Belém. Municipal island lines (Combu, Cotijuba, Mosqueiro) come on top of this figure.

demand_signals.label: Peak-month terminal flow
demand_signals.value: >300,000 people projected through the Belém, Tamandaré and Icoaraci terminals in July 2026 alone
demand_signals.note: July is the local beach-holiday month — island lines surge to Cotijuba, Mosqueiro and Marajó.

demand_signals.label: New terminal wave (COP30 legacy)
demand_signals.value: Three terminals rebuilt or opened in 2025: the R$53M / 4,800 m² Terminal Hidroviário de Belém, the R$7.9M Icoaraci tourist terminal (~2,000 boardings/day expected), and the new Tamandaré terminal
demand_signals.note: Brand-new berths, ticketing halls and waterfront parks — the shoreside infrastructure is done; the vessels are the unmodernised half.

demand_signals.label: COP30 investment
demand_signals.value: ~R$4.7 billion invested in Belém for COP30, including the R$568M Porto Futuro II waterfront restoration and a port warehouse converted into a conference waterway terminal expecting 190,000+ passengers
demand_signals.note: The conference put Amazon river mobility on the world stage — and left the waterfront rebuilt for what comes next.

demand_signals.label: Combu restaurant island
demand_signals.value: Dozens of over-water restaurants line Ilha do Combu's shore, 15 minutes across the Guamá river, served by hourly cooperative lanchas at R$12 a leg
demand_signals.note: Belém's favourite lunch is already a boat ride — a dense, all-year, short-hop premium use case inside an environmental protection area.

use_cases.title: Modernise the geladão
use_cases.body: Belém already runs a public water-bus network — the air-conditioned 'Geladão Fluvial' to Cotijuba and Mosqueiro and hourly lanchas to Barcarena. Clean, smooth foiling shuttles on the same lines from the same brand-new terminals upgrade an adopted habit rather than creating one.

use_cases.title: Combu and the waterfront spider
use_cases.body: Silent short hops from Estação das Docas and Praça Princesa Isabel to Combu's over-water restaurants and the Guamá igarapés — zero-wake and near-silent inside the island's environmental protection area, where every visitor already arrives by boat.

use_cases.title: Barcarena industrial shuttle
use_cases.body: The Belém–Barcarena lancha is one of the state's busiest lines, feeding one of the world's largest alumina complexes at Vila do Conde. A fast, reliable foiling commuter service turns a 45–60 minute tide-dependent crossing into a smooth scheduled half-hour.

use_cases.title: Marajó gateway
use_cases.body: The world's largest river island sits across the bay — today a 2-hour lancha to Soure or a ~3-hour vehicle ferry from Icoaraci to Camará. A foiling service makes the buffalo island a smooth, quiet day trip and anchors the longer Amazon network.

journeys.today: Queue at the busy terminal, pick your restaurant at boarding, then a 15-minute diesel lancha putter across the Guamá.
journeys.with_navier: A silent foiling hop that leaves no wake in the protected island's igarapés — lunch on the Amazon, minutes from downtown.

journeys.today: An hourly ~62-passenger lancha, 45–60 minutes depending on the tide, R$18 — the daily route for commuters, patients and traders.
journeys.with_navier: A foiling shuttle flying above the bay chop cuts the crossing toward half an hour, smooth enough to work or sleep through, with no diesel plume down the Furo das Onças.

journeys.from: Terminal Hidroviário de Belém (Luiz Rebelo Neto)
journeys.today: A 2-hour, 200-seat fast lancha (R$61) or a ~3-hour ship — a pounding open-bay ride when the Baía do Marajó kicks up.
journeys.with_navier: A foiling crossing that flies above the bay's short chop: the same journey, dramatically smoother and quieter, with zero local emissions arriving at the buffalo island.

journeys.today: Ride to Icoaraci then a 20-minute 'geladão' water-bus (R$4.60), or the new direct line — over an hour end-to-end from the centre.
journeys.with_navier: A direct 12 nm foiling link from the rebuilt downtown terminal to the car-free island's trapiche — beach mornings that don't start with a bus ride.

journeys.today: A 70 km drive across the bridge in weekend beach traffic, or the weekend-only water-bus taking about 1h40.
journeys.with_navier: A scheduled foiling express up the Baía do Guajará to the freshwater beaches — under an hour, every day, from the city's showcase waterfront.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The dense inner network is made for the all-electric envelope: Combu (~1.3 nm), Estação das Docas–Combu (~4.5 nm), Icoaraci–Cotijuba (~4.5 nm), Outeiro (~1 nm) — short, sheltered, high-frequency hops from brand-new terminals with grid power, inside waters where zero wake and near-silence matter to riverside communities.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Belém is the gateway to the wider Amazon delta. Beyond the 70 nm electric envelope lie the state's long-haul lines — Cametá up the Tocantins (~80 nm) and Breves in the Marajó archipelago (~100+ nm) — where Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range operates with no charging-infrastructure dependency, extending the network deep into communities that today ride overnight boats.
navier_fit.n35_shuttle: The scheduled backbone: Belém–Barcarena (~11 nm), Belém–Cotijuba (~12 nm), Belém–Mosqueiro (~19 nm), Icoaraci–Camará (~24 nm) and Belém–Soure (~48 nm) match the N35's 12–15 seat scheduled-service profile, shallow 1.5 ft draft for trapiche berths, and DC fast charging at the rebuilt terminals.

competitive_landscape: The water is already run at scale by conventional diesel operators — cooperative lanchas to Combu, the municipal 'Geladão Fluvial' catamarans to Cotijuba and Mosqueiro, Arapari Navegação's hourly Barcarena lanchas, Master Motors and Banav fast lanchas to Marajó, and the Icoaraci–Camará vehicle ferry. That is the strongest possible demand evidence: 550k+ intermunicipal passengers a year plus dense municipal island traffic, all on slow or noisy tonnage. The pain is speed on the longer lines, pounding and spray on the open-bay crossings, diesel noise and wake in protected igarapés, and tide-dependent schedules — exactly what a foiling fleet improves without needing a single new pier.
seasonality: Equatorial and sheltered: the Baía do Guajará is riverine water with no cyclone exposure and a year-round operating window. The Amazonian 'winter' (roughly December–May) brings intense afternoon downpours; June–November is drier. Demand peaks are sharp and predictable: July school holidays flood the island lines (>300k terminal passengers projected for July 2026 alone), October brings the Círio de Nazaré — one of the world's largest religious festivals, with its own river procession on the bay — and the COP30 legacy has extended the international season. Operational notes are riverine rather than maritime: strong tidal currents, and floating vegetation after heavy rains, favour modern sensing and foiling clearance over conventional hulls.
regulatory_note: State waterway passenger transport is regulated by ARTRAN/PA (successor to ARCON-PA), with terminals owned and operated by CPH — the Companhia de Portos e Hidrovias do Estado do Pará — which has just delivered the new Belém, Icoaraci and Tamandaré terminals. Municipal island lines run under the Prefeitura de Belém. Vessel certification and crewing sit with the Brazilian Navy (Capitania dos Portos da Amazônia Oriental), and federal waterway services with ANTAQ. Ilha do Combu is a state environmental protection area (APA), giving silent, zero-wake operations a concrete regulatory audience — and the COP30 legacy agenda gives the state a standing mandate to showcase clean Amazon mobility.
signature_routes: Praça Princesa Isabel ↔ Ilha do Combu (the Amazon restaurant-island hop, zero-wake in the APA)
Belém ↔ Soure/Salvaterra, Marajó (the buffalo-island express across the Baía do Marajó)
Belém ↔ Mosqueiro (the beach express up the Baía do Guajará)
Tamandaré ↔ Barcarena (the working commuter line to the industrial hub)

precedents.why_it_matters: Proof that a foiling fleet can be the transport layer of a water-first territory at national scale — the playbook for a delta capital whose boats already carry the daily load.

The state has already done the hard part — R$4.7bn of urban preparation including three new passenger terminals and the Porto Futuro II waterfront. New-generation vessels are the natural next chapter of a rebuild the world watched.
